19975-base-ball:
John Montgomery Ward wrote Base Ball as an insider's guide to the young professional game. Ward pitched and played shortstop for the New York club. He opens with the doubtful circumstances of the ball's own invention. History's accuracy about the first ball, he jokes, is itself in doubt. From there he treats rules, positions, and the game's growth. Ward was a Columbia-trained lawyer as well as a star.

Ward later helped found the players' Brotherhood and a rebel league. His book is both manual and manifesto for the sport. It dates from 1888, when baseball was becoming big business. Players' rights simmer under his technical chapters. Historians of the game still quote Ward constantly. He remains the thinking ballplayer of his century.
20058-the-napoleon-of-notting-hill:
G. K. Chesterton wrote The Napoleon of Notting Hill, his first novel, set in a future London. The sample verse speaks of starry streets that point to God. It names the great grey water-tower on Campden Hill. A child dreams that epic hour and dreams it still, the poem says.

Chesterton imagines a king who makes each London borough guard its own pride. Notting Hill then takes that game of flags and walls in earnest. The book mixes farce, swordplay, and deep talk about place and loyalty. It has drawn fans of both comic tales and serious ideas ever since.
20163-the-jolliest-school-of-all:
Angela Brazil published The Jolliest School of All in 1922, a girls' school story. A girl empties the bottom cupboards of a big bookcase at speed. Her method is not tidy at all, the book admits freely. Soon books, papers, paint-boxes, and music lie in a jumble around her.

Brazil wrote dozens of school tales loved by girls for decades. Her schools are bright, loyal, and full of scrapes and games. Chalks, stamps, crests, and knitting wool show a schoolgirl's full world. Readers get classic Brazil: cheer, friendship, and school pride in full flood.
20245-a-narrative-of-some-of-the-lord-s-:
George Müller of Bristol told, in his Narrative, of the Lord's dealings with him. Müller built orphan houses run on prayer and gifts alone. A reader from 1844 would not know how the work has grown since. By the time of writing, it had grown three or four times larger.

And still it kept growing, Müller reports with calm wonder. He never made direct appeals for money, by his own firm rule. Food, funds, and helpers came, he believed, in answer to prayer. Readers get a famed record of faith, charity, and Victorian orphan care.
20379-a-narrative-of-some-of-the-lord-s-:
George Müller of Bristol became famous for running orphan homes while refusing to ask anyone for money. He wrote this narrative to tell how God had led him, step by step, through his life and work. He says many souls were blessed by what he told them in person.

Müller felt it his duty to print the account so others, whom he could never meet, might gain from it too. The book records answers to prayer, hard trials, and steady trust. It remains a key first-hand record of one of the best-known faith missions of the Victorian age.
20416-the-annual-catalogue-1737-or-a-new:
The Annual Catalogue for 1737 lists the books published in Britain that year, with short accounts of many titles. Such catalogues helped booksellers and readers track the flood of new print. Each entry gives a taste of the book it names.

Among the lives on offer are memoirs of Madame de Brinvilliers, who poisoned her father and two brothers. Another book tells of an impostor who fooled a man's wife and family, and puzzled the Parliament of France for a long time. Crime, scandal, and wonders sold well in 1737, and the list proves it.
20480-palmistry-for-all:
Palmistry for All, by the famous palmist Cheiro, teaches readers to read character from the hand. Cheiro promised a skill anyone could pick up. His method rested on the lines, mounts, and shapes of the palm.

The book aims at quick, practical judgments. Many readers, it says, want to gain at a mere glance a grasp of the leading traits of people they meet. Businessmen and hosts alike were told the hand would not lie. Cheiro's guides sold widely, and this one shows the rules by which a generation tried to read strangers at sight.
20634-the-sleeping-bard-or-visions-of-th:
Elis Wyn's The Sleeping Bard is a Welsh classic, first written in the early eighteenth century. Its full title promises visions of the world, death, and hell. A bard falls asleep and is carried in dream through each realm in turn, seeing the fates of men.

Scholars have traced where Wyn found his plan. The idea of the Vision of the World, this study shows, was clearly taken from an earlier prose vision. The Vision of Death came from another, and the Vision of Hell from the sties of Pluto. The English text lets new readers judge the fierce Welsh satire for themselves.
20749-st-ronan-s-well:
Sir Walter Scott published St. Ronan's Well in the 1820s, and the 1894 text keeps its period praise. Critics quoted here hail its character work and well-told story. Names like Lady Penelope, MacTurk, and Touchwood fill the cast at a spa town.

Scott sets pride, love, and scandal loose in a fashionable watering place. A secret from the past poisons hope for more than one figure. The novel is his only tale set in his own day, which makes it stand apart. Readers see Scott turn his sharp eye from old battles to drawing-room wars instead.
21050-the-master-of-the-shell:
A nasty house-master, trapped, tied, and left all night in a boot box, fronts The Master of the Shell. No boy will own the deed when daylight brings the reckoning, Reed notes. Talbot Baines Reed sets that bold prank near his school tale's heart.

The Shell, a famed form (class) at St. Domingo's, and its master drive the plot. Boys test a new master's worth by prank, sulk, and slow respect. Reed turns school lore into a tale of character on both sides. The Master of the Shell ranks high in his school canon, shrewd about boys and the men who earn their trust.
21376-will-of-the-mill:
In a Derbyshire dale with a Huguenot past, the vicar's son and the silk mill owner's son are fast friends in George Manville Fenn's tale. A visiting artist lodging with a mill worker falls down an old mine shaft, and the boys find him before the rescue party arrives. Then the mill catches fire in the night.

The fire pump has been disabled, and only just repaired in time by the artist's host, a man named Drinkwater, in French Boileau. Drinkwater goes mad with hatred for the mill owner, and suspicion falls on him for the fire. When autumn rains burst the mill dam and flood the village, the question of his guilt drives a dramatic finish.
21480-sunshine-bill:
Bill, son of a Portsmouth wherryman and an apple seller, loses his father in W. H. G. Kingston's Sunshine Bill. The harbour accident leaves a large, cheerful family hard pressed to eat and dress. Captain Trevelyan then offers Bill a boy seaman's place in his ship, the Lilly.

Bill sails knowing four years may pass before he sees home again. His messmate Tommy Rebow is a weaker lad, and the crew are decent folk. Hurricanes, men overboard, fights with the French, sharks, and short rations test them all. Thanks to God marks each escape in this warm, gritty tale.
21667-hollowmell:
E. R. Burden sends a schoolgirl on a mission in Hollowmell, or A Schoolgirl's Mission, printed at Glasgow in 1881. Minnie Kimberley hunts her lost books through cupboards, desks, and under tables. Her books always turn up in the least likely places, as her friends well know.

Minnie's plan grows through preparations and a first essay at doing good. A dispute is settled, Mona suffers defeat, and a success crowns the work. The tale runs short, some nine chapters from plan to end. The Society style of improving fiction shapes it, with Minnie's bright face and quick temper giving it life.
22034-a-narrative-of-some-of-the-lord-s-:
George Müller of Bristol became famous for running orphan houses on faith alone. He never asked any person for money, yet thousands of orphans were fed and housed. His Narrative of Some of the Lord's Dealings, written by himself, tells how it happened. This second part continues the record of his personal life and work.

Müller describes the doubts that tested him when he first published his account. He tells of the Scriptural Knowledge Institution and its schools, Bibles, and missionaries. Day by day entries note sums received, often at the last hour. The book became a classic of its kind, read wherever Christians spoke of answered prayer.
22066-the-long-roll:
Mary Johnston of Virginia published The Long Roll in 1911 as the first of two novels on the war between the States. A wintry day opens the tale: the small town breathes hard with excitement. It might have climbed rapidly from lower land, so heightened are its pulses and so wide its prospect. Old red-brick houses and leafless trees look out between the mountain ranges as Virginia moves toward war.

Johnston follows her Virginians into Stonewall Jackson's campaigns. She had researched the war for years and wrote battle as few novelists could. Romance runs beside the marching in her stately prose. The Long Roll was a bestseller and fixed the Shenandoah war in popular memory.
22128-bessie-costrell:
Mrs. Humphry Ward, the best-selling author of Robert Elsmere, wrote the novella Bessie Costrell in 1895. The scene is Clinton Magna, an English village, at harvest time. An old labourer counts this his last harvest after fifty-six years of work, man and boy. A curious pleasure stirs him at the thought of change, though age has bent him.

Into this village world comes Bessie, and with her the money that tests every bond. Ward watches trust, thrift, and temptation work on simple lives. The tale is short, close, and unsparing. It is often counted among Ward's finest pieces of fiction, a village tragedy told without melodrama.
22148-a-narrative-of-some-of-the-lord-s-:
The third part of George Müller's Narrative of the Lord's Dealings with him carries his famous record forward. Müller, who ran Bristol's orphan houses without ever asking for money, published each part for the same reason. He wanted readers to see that God still answered prayer in ordinary days. This part's preface repeats the reasons given for the second.

Accounts run here to the end of 1840 for the orphan houses. Personal matters continue a little further. Entries list gifts received, needs met, and children housed, almost day by day. Together the parts form one of the most read faith memoirs of the Victorian age, still printed by the Müller charities.
22163-the-rover-boys-on-the-farm-or-last:
Arthur M. Winfield, Edward Stratemeyer's pen name, wrote The Rover Boys on the Farm as a late Putnam Hall story. The subtitle calls it Last Days at Putnam Hall, and the boys know their schooling is ending. Rover adventures here mix school rivalry with farm life. Friends join the brothers for adventures, some comical and some strange and mystifying.

At school the old rivalries burn as keen as ever. On the farm, mysteries and practical jokes take over the plot. The Rovers prove their worth more than once, as the preface promises. The volume closes a long chapter of the series, sending its heroes toward the wider world of the later books.
22171-the-radiant-shell:
Paul Ernst wrote The Radiant Shell, a science fiction tale printed in Astounding Stories in January 1932. Ernst was a German-American engineer who turned to pulp writing. His story opens in a hushed conference room. White-faced men stare at each other across the table, weighing an incredible report: a world in which there is no United States of America.

A man on a metal plate is seen vanishing in the cover picture's scene. Parallel worlds and secret weapons drive Ernst's plot in the early pulp style. The tale mixes politics with dimension-hopping wonder. It survives as a sample of the brash, idea-first fiction that built American science fiction's first generation of fans.
23009-a-modern-idyll:
A practiced voice performs in A Modern Idyll, a story by Frank Harris. It is not probable you will hear many more from me, the speaker says. A shade of sadness enters his lower tone as he ends the phrase. He lets the sad note drift in unconsciously, though long practice has made him an artist in managing his voice.

Harris watches that artistry the way a duelist watches hands. His idyll is modern because its lovers, if lovers they are, act their feelings as much as feel them. Sincerity becomes the story's open question. The prose stays smooth and slightly cold, matching its subject. Readers who enjoy psychological fencing in period dress will find this brief tale neatly made.
23221-the-story-of-the-little-mamsell:
Charlotte Niese's The Story of the Little Mamsell is told through a child's memories of an old storyteller. As a girl, the narrator spent coins from her own slender pocket money to coax the old man into telling his tales. She was not always successful in buying a story.

He had gloomy spells and said almost nothing. On better days, he shared tales from his own past freely, and his life had not lacked variety. Niese frames the little mamsell's story inside that exchange: a child's eagerness set against an old man's silence, memory, and hard-won tales.
a-boy-s-will: Robert Frost's 1913 A Boy's Will: his first book of poems. "The road not taken" is still ahead. The essential American poet begins. Frost's first poems, the poet begins, the essential American poet begins, his first book.
a-romance-of-billy-goat-hill: Alice Hegan Rice — beloved author of Mrs. Wiggs of the Cabbage Patch — sets this romance on Billy-Goat Hill, where a poor but proud Kentucky family guards its dignity. A young woman's heart and a neighborhood's prejudices collide in a story full of local color. Rice's affection for her characters shines on every page.
all-s-well-that-ends-well: Shakespeare's bittersweet "problem play": the clever Helena wins the husband she loves through a bed-trick, then must win his heart as well. Darker than the great comedies and stranger than the tragedies, it asks whether ends really justify means. Fascinating and unsettling in equal measure.
b09-luther-bondage-will:
On the Bondage of the Will, from 1525, is Martin Luther's answer to Erasmus, the famed Dutch scholar. Erasmus had defended free will in his Diatribe, and Luther replied at length and without mercy. The Latin work argues that the human will, in matters of salvation, is bound and cannot turn itself to God.

Grace, in Luther's account, must do the whole work, or it is not grace at all. He praised the book in later years as his finest, a rare claim from him. Edward Thomas Vaughan's 1823 English rendering carries the text here. The debate with Erasmus still anchors talks on freedom, fate, and faith.
black-heart-and-white-heart-a-zulu-idyll: H. Rider Haggard's 1900 Black Heart and White Heart: a Zulu idyll of love and war. Exotic and tragic in his grand manner. Vintage Haggard, zulu love amid tribal war, haggard's exotic tragedy, Haggard's exotic African tragedy.

govdocs-archive_org-nsia-DurhamBill_Durh:
Bill Durham wrote to Harold Weisberg on May 27, 1975 about a small object with large meaning: Lee Harvey Oswald's notebook. The letter discusses names found in it, including FBI agent James Hosty and a Gandy. A notebook page naming the agent who knew Oswald before the shooting was evidence worth arguing over.

Durham also takes up J. Edgar Hoover's notification of Robert Kennedy and claims made by former FBI agent Joseph Schott. The letter moves the way researcher mail did, lead by lead, through the open questions of the case. It preserves that exchange between two men still working the file in 1975.

govdocs-archive_org-nsia-MoyersBill_Moye:
A Washington Post magazine page presents Bill Moyers in his own words and in pictures. Moyers had been President Johnson's press secretary and a central aide. One line from the page is quoted in the file: 'We won the civil rights battles of the '60s, but lost the political war.' A photograph shows Moyers with Johnson in 1964.

Moyers left the White House and became a publisher and then a television journalist. The page belongs to his years of looking back at the Johnson era he served. govdocs-archive_org-nsia-RaysAll_Rays_Al:
James Earl Ray signed this application for a pardon on October 6, 1980. He filed it with the Tennessee Board of Paroles. Ray was prisoner number 65477 at Brushy Mountain Prison. He was serving his sentence for the assassination of Martin Luther King Jr., to which he had pleaded guilty in 1969.

Ray spent the rest of his life trying to undo that plea. He claimed he was a patsy in a larger plot and asked courts and boards, again and again, for a trial or a pardon. This application is one formal round of that campaign. It preserves his prisoner number, his prison, and his request in his own filing, twelve years after the murder.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-SartorBill_Sart:
An FBI memorandum records Robert Patrick Lyons's account of meeting Bill Sartor. Lyons met Sartor through a woman named Marie Geisandorf. The meeting happened after the death of Martin Luther King Jr. Sartor was a figure whose name drew agents' attention in the King case's wide net.

Memos like this one log introductions: who met whom, through whom, and when. In a case built on possible conspiracies, introductions were evidence, the joints where a plot would have to connect. Lyons's account gives the bureau one such joint, dated after the assassination. The memorandum preserves it in the standard form, a small link kept because no one could yet say which links mattered.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-Windowsill_Wind: Only a fragment of an article on the James Earl Ray case survives here. It touches on Ray's guilty plea and his later escape. govdocs-nsarchive-Briefing_Book_cyber-va: Cybersecurity: When Hackers Went to the Hill - the National Security Archive briefing-book page capture revisiting the hackers' account before Congress. The archivists capture, complete. A single capture. Dated entry. From the archive shelves, for readers.
govdocs-nsarchive-News_foia_Federal_Judg: On October 4, 2019, a federal judge ordered the White House to preserve records of the president's calls with foreign heads of state. govdocs-nsarchive-News_foia_The_Capitol_:
Donald Trump's official call log for January 6, 2021 has a gap of more than seven hours while the Capitol was under attack. In June 2022, the House January 6 committee opened televised hearings. The National Security Archive then published this account of its chronology work, and of the questions raised by that missing stretch of the president's day.

One puzzle anchors the posting. A phone call absent from the official log still showed up in the end-of-day diary. So how did it get there, and what else is missing? Call records matter because they can show who a president spoke with while events unfolded. Readers get a focused look at a documentary gap, the evidence around its edges, and why archivists treat a blank space in the record as a finding in itself.
how-to-tell-stories-to-children-and-some: Sara Bryant's guide (1905) teaches parents the art of storytelling well. It includes sample tales to practice nightly. The Tower library holds the full text. jack-and-jill: Louisa May Alcott's 1880 Jack and Jill: two children's friendship and recovery. Warm and moral, it charmed young readers. A beloved Alcott. Jack and Jill's friendship endures, alcott's children, warmly drawn, Alcott's children warmly and truly drawn.
jimmy-lucy-and-all:
Jimmy, Lucy, and All is a children's story book by Sophie May, issued in Boston in 1900. It belongs to her Little Prudy's Children set, alongside the Little Prudy, Dotty Dimple, and Flaxie Frizzle series. The title page lists Lee and Shepard as publishers. Chapter titles promise a tallyho ride, a first dinner, and Lucy's gold mine. A zebra kitten, a stolen chimney, and a thief found keep the fun moving. One chapter turns on begging pardon, and another on the little schoolma'am's earthquake. Nate's cave and Jimmy's good luck close the book. larry-dexter-s-great-search-or-the-hunt-:
Howard R. Garis published Larry Dexter's Great Search in New York in 1909. Its subtitle is The Hunt for the Missing Millionaire. Garis also wrote the Dick Hamilton books for boys.

Larry Dexter works as a young reporter in this series. A missing millionaire gives him a case to chase. The frontispiece shows Larry crying out that he has found something. Clues, travel, and rival hunters keep the pace quick. Garis wrote for boys who liked newsroom adventure mixed with mystery. Garis fills the hunt with newspaper work and quick travel. lemorne-versus-huell:
Elizabeth Stoddard published Lemorne Versus Huell in Harper's Magazine in 1863. The narrator spends two months at Newport with her Aunt Eliza Huell. Those months, she says, created all that is dramatic in her destiny.

Aunt Eliza came to the seaside for her health. She was also caught in a lawsuit, which made her troublesome company. The niece serves her from duty more than affection. A legal fight gives the tale its very title. Stoddard's sharp eye turns a family visit into quiet drama. Newport's shore setting cools a story of family friction. Stoddard's narrator watches more than she speaks, to sharp effect.
love-conquers-all:
Love Conquers All is a book of comic essays by Robert Benchley, printed in 1922. Gluyas Williams drew the pictures that go with the jokes. Contents promise family life in America and rules for watching auction bridge. Benchley also tells how to watch a chess match and a baseball game.

He asks whether insects think, and what to do while the family is away. Every piece takes a small, dull subject and makes it absurd. Benchley's mock-serious voice is the real show in each essay. He was one of America's best-loved humorists between the wars. These short pieces still raise laughs a century later.
ma-pettengill:
Ma Pettengill is a book of comic Western tales by Harry Leon Wilson. Wilson, who wrote Ruggles of Red Gap, published it in 1919. The narrator strolls up from the Arrowhead corrals on a Sunday afternoon. His hostess, Mrs. Lysander John Pettengill, sits knitting on the ranch piazza.

Ma runs her ranch and her neighbors with a firm, funny hand. Stories here tell of a love affair, a vendetta, and a porch wren. Red Gap's big-league pretensions get their share of teasing. Wilson writes in a dry, drawling, very American voice. Ma Pettengill stands among his best-loved comic creations. The book is pure pleasure for lovers of Western humor.
maastricht-treaty-1992-full:
The Maastricht Treaty is the 1992 agreement that founded the European Union. Its full text runs from a preamble through seven titles and many protocols. Title I states common provisions for the member states. Later titles amend the treaties of the European Communities.

The treaty creates a common foreign and security policy. It also joins the states in justice and home affairs work. Protocols set rules for the future European Central Bank. Others fix deficit limits and the tests for joining the euro. Denmark's property rights get a protocol of their own. Few documents have reshaped modern Europe more deeply. This is the complete legal text, article by article.
milly-darrell:
Mary Elizabeth Braddon, the Victorian novelist of Lady Audley's Secret, wrote Milly Darrell as a serial story. It ran in the magazine Belgravia from November 1870 to January 1871. This Paris printing of 1873, in Asher's Collection of English Authors, joins it with other stories. The edition was copyrighted for foreign circulation only.

Braddon was among the most popular English novelists of her era. Her sensation fiction turned on secrets, strong feeling, and threatened reputations. Milly Darrell belongs to the shorter tales she supplied to the magazines. Continental editions like this one carried her work to English readers traveling and living abroad.
miss-minerva-and-william-green-hill:
Frances Boyd Calhoun opens this Southern children's tale at a small-town gate at night. Little William Green Hill arrives by bus, riding up front beside the driver, Sam Lamb. His Aunt Minerva waits on the porch, scandalized that he would not ride inside. The boy wipes her kiss and claims he is only rubbing it in.

Billy, as he insists on being called, has run wild on a plantation until now. Miss Minerva intends to raise him by her strict rules. Calhoun tells the clash in rich dialect and gentle comedy. A Major's name makes the spinster blush, hinting at romance for her as well.
mr-hogarth-s-will:
Catherine Helen Spence wrote this novel about a death, a will, and two young women left in doubt. Mr. Hogarth of Cross Hall, in rural Scotland, dies suddenly in the early 1850s. He had raised two orphan nieces as his own daughters. The opening chapter gathers mourners to hear what his will will do.

Hogarth was known as odd and strict, yet fond of his nieces. He trusted women in theory but ruled the girls with many limits. Their schooling was shaped to fit his own views. The will sets the story's test of character, money, and freedom. Spence uses one household to probe how women could live and choose.
mr-meeson-s-will:
H. Rider Haggard's novel turns on a will, a shipwreck, and a fight in court. The contents name Augusta, her publisher Meeson's, and young Eustace. Eustace is cut off early, and Augusta sails on the Kangaroo. A wreck strands the party on Kerguelen Land.

Back in England the tale becomes a legal battle. Chapter titles promise lawyers, flight, and a case called Meeson v. Addison. Augusta holds the key to who gets the fortune. Haggard mixes sea adventure with courtroom drama. The odd will at the center tests greed, loyalty, and love under hard pressure.
nasa-tm-19660011811-prime-minitrack-and-:
Hans G Hertz at Goddard compared two ways of tracking the Vanguard II satellite in this report. One way is Prime Minitrack, which listens to the satellite's radio transmitter. The other is the Baker-Nunn camera, which photographs the satellite against the stars. Data cover twenty-six days while the transmitter still worked, in 1959. In all, hundreds of observations from both systems are presented.

Only readings made at the same time by both systems are used for the comparison. That pairing gives a fair test of accuracy. Tracking accuracy decides how well an orbit is known. Hertz's study helped judges weigh radio tracking against camera tracking, at the dawn of the satellite age.
nasa-tm-19680018321-nasa-lrc-program-to-:
Langley Research Center staff outline a program to define Earth's infrared horizon by direct experiment. Infrared horizon sensors steer spacecraft by watching the edge of Earth glow in heat light. To design such sensors well, engineers first need flight measurements of that horizon's true brightness pattern, called its radiance signature.

Flights on the X-15 research aircraft gathered data in three bands of the infrared spectrum. A second effort, Project Scanner, measured the horizon in two spectral bands. The report also weighs a larger flight program to widen coverage beyond both efforts. Its stated goal is sensor accuracy near one hundredth of a degree in judging vertical direction.
nasa-tm-19700025113-spectral-responses-o:
Henry W. Brandhorst Jr. and Russell E. Hart Jr. of the Lewis Research Center wrote this paper for a 1970 solar cell conference in Seattle. It measures how silicon solar cells respond to light at low temperatures. Cells on deep-space craft can grow very cold.

The team measured responses for cells that did well in the cold and cells that did poorly. Poor cells showed a faulty rear contact or a flat spot in their output curve, they report. Their current also fell fast as the temperature dropped. Good cells lost output in a slow, even way. The authors hope the contrast points to better cold-weather cells.
nasa-tm-19720004062-flight-investigation:
Richard R Burley of the Lewis Research Center flew this nozzle study in November 1971, as NASA TM X-2396. An auxiliary inlet ejector nozzle sat on an engine nacelle under a wing. Burley warned that air reaching a mounted nozzle differs from clean tunnel flow. A podded engine near the wing's lower rear surface was the case of general interest. Flight tests could show what the mounting really did to performance.

Nozzle behavior alone in a tunnel can mislead designers. The wing, nacelle, and passing airflow all reshape the stream the nozzle breathes. Burley's flights measured the installed case directly. Programs building ejector nozzles for supersonic cruise aircraft needed such data. The report belongs to a wider Lewis effort on these nozzles.
nightfall:
Anthony Pryde opens Nightfall in a dark manor house called Wanhope, on a June afternoon. Laura Clowes comes in from the garden to tell Bernard that tea is ready. It is five o'clock, yet the hall is so dark she must grope her way through it.

Wanhope has a plain brick front and a great gateway of weathered stone. The family arms and motto, Fortis et Fidelis, are carved there. Inside, Spanish chestnut wood lines floor, stairs, walls, and ceiling. Flemish glass dims the light still more. A wall of old weapons, armour, and blades from many lands gives the hall its one glint.
oslo-accords-1993-full:
Signed on September 13, 1993, the Declaration of Principles on Interim Self-Government Arrangements is the founding text of the Oslo Accords between the Government of Israel and the Palestine Liberation Organization. Its opening declares an end to decades of confrontation and a mutual recognition of legitimate and political rights, with a just, lasting, and comprehensive peace as the stated goal.

The articles provide for free elections to a Palestinian council under international observation, with Palestinian police keeping public order in the West Bank and Gaza Strip. A five-year transitional period begins with withdrawal from Gaza and Jericho. Permanent status talks, covering Jerusalem, refugees, settlements, security, and borders, must start by the third year. The document framed Middle East diplomacy for a generation.
project-gutenberg-complete-works-of-wins:

Named works include Richard Carvel, The Crisis, Coniston, The Inside of the Cup, Mr. Crewe's Career, and A Far Country, plus a play and an essay on democracy. The set opens with The Crossing, a tale of the old border country. Readers get the whole shelf of a once-famous writer in one place.
puck-of-pook-s-hill:
Rudyard Kipling wrote a set of linked tales for children in which Puck, the old spirit of England, calls up figures from the land's past. Stories and songs alternate, each tale tied to the Sussex hill country where two children act out a play.

The contents run from Weland's Sword and Sir Richard's Norman knights to a Roman centurion on the Great Wall, Pictish raiders, a smuggler's tale, and a final story of treasure and law. Songs by Puck, the Danes, and the children thread the book. Readers get English history told as magic, memory, and adventure.
sophocles-seven-plays-campbell:
Sophocles of Athens wrote the seven tragedies that survive complete from his large output. Lewis Campbell translated all seven into English verse. Oedipus Rex, Antigone, and Electra lead a set that defined tragedy itself.

Oedipus hunts the killer who polluted Thebes and finds himself. Antigone buries her brother against the king's decree and accepts death. Ajax, the Trachiniae, Philoctetes, and Oedipus at Colonus complete the surviving plays. Sophocles balances irony, character, and fate with unmatched control. Campbell's dignified verse served English readers for generations. No shelf of Greek drama feels complete without these seven plays.
the-coming-of-bill: Wodehouse's comedy turns on Bill — a baby whose arrival upends the lives, romances, and ambitions of the adults around him. Custody battles and love affairs tangle in the author's inimitable style. A lesser-known Wodehouse, but pure delight for his fans.
the-courtship-of-susan-bell: Trollope's The Courtship of Susan Bell is a Saratoga romance. A lovely young beauty weighs two very different suitors with care. The charming novelette glows throughout with gentle irony. American manners seen through amused English eyes.

theophrastus-on-stones-hill:
